newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia economy seen strong but exports worrying.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia economy seen strong but exports worrying.

text.p: Indonesia's latest macroeconomic figures indicate its economy is buoyant and inflation is under control, but slow growth in non-oil exports is slightly worrying, economists said on Thursday.

The government announced on Wednesday that the consumer price index fell 0.17 percent month-on-month in June, after a 0.19 percent rise in May, while annual inflation slipped to 4.98 percent from 5.08 percent.

It also said Indonesia, the only Asian member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries, recorded an April trade surplus of $590.5 million, rising from $243.3 million in March and $366.2 million in April 1996.
Exports rose to $4.153 billion in April from $4.064 billion in March, while oil and gas exports rose to $968.5 million from $960.9 million.
"However, non-oil export growth, which is being keenly watched by the market, continued its sluggish trend of growth," the Singapore-based I.D.E.A. consultancy said in a commentary.
"We note that non-oil exports in April 1996 grew 22 percent year-on-year, and has been on a downtrend ever since," it said, adding that growth in April 1997 was 3.1 percent on an annual basis.

"Indonesia loses out to cheaper cost centres like China and Vietnam in this respect, as exports are not high enough up the value-added ladder," it said. "Attempts to move up the ladder quickly will be necessary to ensure sustainability of the rapid growth trend."
Another economist said he did not expect any real change in the situation until after March next year, when presidential elections are to be held.
"It's a lame-duck government," said Christianto Wibisono, director of the Indonesian Business Data Centre, referring to the ruling Golkar party's sweeping win in the May 29 general elections.
He said since the new cabinet would be formed only after the presidential elections, it was unlikely that new policies to boost exports would be formulated in the meantime.
Ng Bok Eng, regional economist with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Singapore, said he was not overly concerned about non-oil exports.

"Non-oil exports have not been doing particularly well, but that's not just Indonesia, its right across the region," he told Reuters. "I would not be too hasty to suggest that this is a structural problem, it could be a cyclical problem that all the other regional economies are also facing."
He said the inflation figures were encouraging and added the government would not have much difficulty in keeping annual inflation under its targeted six percent in 1997.

Food prices, the largest constituent in the price index, had risen 6.5 percent year-on-year in June after a May rise of 6.8 percent, but it was still the second-highest surge for the past 10 months, Ng said.
But he added: "I am not too concerned about food prices. That has been pretty well managed by BULOG (the state commodities regulator)."

"Generally the (Indonesian) economy is in good shape," he added. "The non-oil exports I expect to pick up by the later part of this year. Even with very weak non-oil exports, we are getting a sizeable surplus so that must be an encouragement."
